anchors.exact: Constructed entirely from standard ConvNet modules, ConvNeXts compete favorably with Transformers in terms of accuracy and scalability, achieving 87.8% ImageNet top-1 accuracy and outperforming Swin Transformers on COCO detection and ADE20K segmentation, while maintaining the simplicity and efficiency of standard ConvNets.
Surprisingly, ConvNeXts, constructed entirely from standard ConvNet modules, compete favorably with Transformers in terms of accuracy, scalability and robustness across all major benchmarks.

We propose ConvNeXts, a pure ConvNet model that can compete favorably with state-of-the-art hierarchical vision Transformers across multiple computer vision benchmarks, while retaining the simplicity and efficiency of standard ConvNets.
We demonstrate that a standard ConvNet model can achieve the same level of scalability as hierarchical vision Transformers while being much simpler in design.

nodes.label: ConvNeXts, built only from standard ConvNet modules, compete favorably with hierarchical vision Transformers in accuracy and scalability, reaching 87.8% ImageNet top-1 and matching or beating Swin on COCO and ADE20K, while keeping ConvNet simplicity and efficiency.
nodes.note: The Transformer comparators are almost entirely Swin (plus DeiT/ViT on ImageNet); 'Transformers' in general is broader than what is tested. Code is stated at b3: https://github.com/facebookresearch/ConvNeXt, and the COCO/ADE20K runs use MMDetection/MMSegmentation with Swin's official weights (b284–b285), which a re-run could attempt.
nodes.short: Pure ConvNeXt competes favorably with Transformers

anchors.exact: Many Transformer architectural choices can be incorporated in a ConvNet, and they lead to increasingly better performance. In the end, our pure ConvNet model, named ConvNeXt, can outperform the Swin Transformer.
Intriguingly, a significant portion of the design choices taken in a vision Transformer may be mapped to ConvNet instantiations.
We have finished our first “playthrough” and discovered ConvNeXt, a pure ConvNet, that can outperform the Swin Transformer for ImageNet-1K classification in this compute regime.

nodes.flag: The roadmap is a single sequential path: each modification is evaluated only on top of all previous ones, in one fixed order. No alternative orderings, no removal ablations from the final model, and no interaction tests are reported, so the accuracy credited to any individual step depends on where it sits in the chain. Closing this would need ablations that remove each component from the final ConvNeXt.
nodes.label: Many Transformer architectural choices can be incorporated into a ConvNet and lead to increasingly better performance, so that a pure ConvNet (ConvNeXt-T) outperforms Swin-T on ImageNet-1K in the same compute regime.
nodes.short: Transformer design choices transfer to ConvNets

anchors.exact: This intermediate step reduces the FLOPs to 4.1G, resulting in a temporary performance degradation to 79.9%.

The network’s performance increases from 79.9% (3×3) to 80.6% (7×7), while the network’s FLOPs stay roughly the same. Additionally, we observe that the benefit of larger kernel sizes reaches a saturation point at 7×7.

nodes.flag: The +0.7% is measured against the intermediate model that had just lost 0.7% by moving the depthwise conv up (80.64→79.92 in Table 10). Relative to the model before that move, the two steps together leave accuracy unchanged (80.64 vs 80.57) while cutting FLOPs from 4.64G to 4.15G, so the gain is an efficiency gain rather than an accuracy gain; the source does not present this net comparison. Table 10 also shows 7×7 and 9×9 identical (80.57) with ±0.14 spread, which is thin support for a precise 7×7 saturation point.
nodes.label: With the depthwise conv moved up, enlarging the kernel from 3×3 to 7×7 raises accuracy from 79.9% to 80.6% at roughly constant FLOPs, and the benefit saturates at 7×7.

anchors.exact: This process improves the result by 0.7% to 81.3%, practically matching the performance of Swin-T.
This further boosts the performance to 81.4%, already surpassing Swin-T’s result.
We observe that our ConvNet model does not have any difficulties training with LN; in fact, the performance is slightly better, obtaining an accuracy of 81.5%.
We can improve the accuracy to 82.0%, significantly exceeding Swin-T’s 81.3%.

nodes.label: Micro-design changes—one GELU per block, fewer normalization layers, LayerNorm in place of BatchNorm, and separate downsampling layers with added LNs—raise accuracy stepwise from 80.6% to 82.0%, exceeding Swin-T's 81.3%.
nodes.note: The source reports that ReLU→GELU alone leaves accuracy unchanged (80.6%) and that separate downsampling initially diverged until normalization layers were added (b93). Several individual steps (81.3→81.4→81.5) are within the ±0.09 seed spread; the source describes them as slight.
nodes.short: Micro design lifts ConvNeXt-T above Swin-T

The source's own thesis is that training techniques account for a large share of ConvNet–Transformer gaps, yet it does not retrain Swin with the ConvNeXt recipe, so part of the 0.6–0.8% margins could be recipe rather than architecture. A same-recipe Swin run would close this.
nodes.label: On ImageNet-1K training, ConvNeXt outperforms Swin Transformers of similar complexity across all sizes, sometimes by a substantial margin (0.8% for Tiny; 0.6% for Base at 384²), with higher inference throughput.

anchors.exact: Across different model complexities, ConvNeXt achieves on-par or better performance than Swin Transformer. When scaled up to bigger models (ConvNeXt-B/L/XL) pre-trained on ImageNet-22K, in many cases ConvNeXt is significantly better (e.g. +1.0 AP) than Swin Transformers in terms of box and mask AP.

nodes.flag: No seed repetition or variance is reported for any COCO run, and the ImageNet-1K-pretrained differences are 0.0–0.2 AP (e.g. Cascade Mask R-CNN Swin-T 50.4 vs ConvNeXt-T 50.4 box AP). The word 'significantly' at the 22K scale is used in the ordinary, not statistical, sense; the +1.0 AP figures come from single runs after a hyper-parameter sweep applied to both models (b285).
nodes.label: On COCO detection and instance segmentation, ConvNeXt backbones achieve on-par or better AP than Swin across sizes, and with ImageNet-22K pre-training the larger ConvNeXt-B/L/XL models are often significantly better (e.g. +1.0 AP).
nodes.short: COCO: on par or better than Swin

anchors.exact: As demon-strated throughout the paper, the inference throughputs of ConvNeXts are comparable to or exceed that of Swin Transformers.
Furthermore, we notice that training ConvNeXts requires less memory than training Swin Transformers.
Swin Transformers and ConvNeXts both achieve faster inference throughput than V100 GPUs, but ConvNeXts’ advantage is now significantly greater, sometimes up to 49% faster.

nodes.label: Despite using depthwise convolutions, ConvNeXt's inference throughput is comparable to or exceeds Swin's, training uses less memory, and on A100 GPUs with TF32 and channels-last layout ConvNeXt is up to 49% faster.
nodes.note: The source itself calls the A100 result 'preliminary' (b394). The training-memory claim rests on a single example (Cascade Mask R-CNN, ConvNeXt-B vs Swin-B). The source also attributes the accuracy-FLOPs advantage over vanilla ViT to the ConvNet inductive bias shared by both ConvNeXt and Swin (b217).
nodes.short: ConvNeXt is as fast or faster than Swin

anchors.exact: Since network complexity is closely correlated with the final performance, the FLOPs are roughly controlled over the course of the exploration, though at intermediate steps the FLOPs might be higher or lower than the reference models. All models are trained and evaluated on ImageNet-1K.

We will use this fixed training recipe with the same hyperparameters throughout the “modernization” process. Each reported accuracy on the ResNet-50 regime is an average obtained from training with three different random seeds.
For experiments in “modernizing a ConvNet” (Section 2), we also use Table 5’s setting for ImageNet-1K, except EMA is disabled, as we find using EMA severely hurts models with BatchNorm layers.
ResNet-50 regime experiments are run with 3 random seeds.

nodes.label: The modernization roadmap trains every variant on ImageNet-1K with one fixed 300-epoch AdamW recipe (Mixup, CutMix, RandAugment, Random Erasing, Stochastic Depth, Label Smoothing; EMA disabled), holds FLOPs only roughly constant, and averages ResNet-50-regime results over three random seeds.
nodes.note: Hyper-parameters are fixed across all steps, so no per-step re-tuning; the source does not say whether the recipe was tuned on the starting ResNet or the ending ConvNeXt. Seed averaging is stated only for the ResNet-50 regime.
nodes.short: Fixed recipe, rough FLOP control, 3 seeds

anchors.exact: The ImageNet-1K dataset consists of 1000 object classes with 1.2M training images. We report ImageNet-1K top-1 accuracy on the validation set.
We train ConvNeXts for 300 epochs using AdamW [46] with a learning rate of 4e-3.
We use Exponential Moving Average (EMA) [51] as we find it alleviates larger models’ overfitting.
We fine-tune ImageNet- 22K pre-trained models on ImageNet-1K for 30 epochs.
ConvNeXt models are trained with the same settings as before, but with longer warmup epochs.
We directly test our

nodes.label: Main ImageNet results use 300-epoch ImageNet-1K training (AdamW, lr 4e-3, batch 4096, EMA, Layer Scale), or 90-epoch ImageNet-22K pre-training followed by 30-epoch ImageNet-1K fine-tuning at 224² or 384²; top-1 is reported on the ImageNet-1K validation set, and the same trained models are tested directly on the robustness benchmarks.
nodes.note: Full hyper-parameters are in Tables 5–6 (b232–b282). Fine-tuning starts from non-EMA weights except for ConvNeXt-L on ImageNet-1K, where the best EMA checkpoint is selected because of overfitting (b257).

anchors.exact: Following Swin Transformer [45], we use multi-scale training, AdamW optimizer, and a 3× schedule.
All model variants are trained for 160K iterations with a batch size of 16.

We conduct a lightweight sweep for COCO experiments including learning rate {1e-4, 2e-4}, layer-wise learning rate decay [6] {0.7, 0.8, 0.9, 0.95}, and stochastic depth rate {0.3, 0.4, 0.5, 0.6, 0.7, 0.8}. We fine-tune the ImageNet-22K pre-trained Swin-B/L on COCO using the same sweep.
ImageNet-1K pre-trained Swin results are from their Github repository [3]. AP numbers of the ResNet-50 and X101 models are from [45]. We measure FPS on an A100 GPU.
Swins’ results are from its GitHub repository [2]. Following Swin, we report mIoU results with multi-scale testing.

nodes.label: Downstream evaluation fine-tunes Mask R-CNN and Cascade Mask R-CNN on COCO (multi-scale training, AdamW, 3× schedule, small hyper-parameter sweep also applied to 22K-pre-trained Swin-B/L) and UperNet on ADE20K (160K iterations, batch 16, multi-scale test mIoU); ImageNet-1K-pretrained Swin numbers are copied from Swin's repositories and FPS is measured on an A100.
nodes.note: Only the 22K-pretrained Swin-B/L COCO runs were re-run by the authors with the same sweep; all other Swin comparators are published numbers. MMDetection and MMSegmentation toolboxes are used (b284).

anchors.exact: Inference throughput is measured on a V100 GPU, following [45].

We now benchmark them on the more advanced A100 GPUs, which support the TensorFloat32 (TF32) tensor cores. We employ PyTorch [50] version 1.10 to use the latest “Channel Last” memory layout [22] for further speedup.

nodes.label: Inference throughput in Table 1 is measured on a V100 GPU following Swin's protocol; Appendix E re-benchmarks on A100 GPUs with TF32 tensor cores and PyTorch 1.10 channels-last memory layout.
nodes.note: The A100 setup uses optimizations (TF32, channels-last) that favour dense convolution; the source does not state whether equivalent optimizations were applied to the Swin implementation.
